draft.title: Beginning in the middle
card: A story often opens with an orientation: who the characters are, where and when it is set. Beginning in the middle skips or delays this and starts in the middle of the action.
The Latin name for this is in medias res, which means "into the middle of things". The first line might be a chase, an argument or a crisis already under way.
The effect on a reader is to pull them in fast. They have questions straight away, such as who is running and why, so they keep reading to find out.
The writer then fills in the background later, in small pieces, once the reader cares about what is happening. Example: "The lock gave way and Priya ran." We learn why after she is already moving.
draft.remember: Start in the action, then supply the background once the reader is hooked.

a.q: A story opens with: "The siren was still wailing when Jo hit the water." Why might the writer open this way?
opts: To hook the reader with action before any background
To explain the setting and characters before any action
To end the story with a calm and settled mood
To show events in strict order from birth onwards
a.why: The opening drops the reader into action with no orientation, so they ask questions and read on. The second option describes a standard orientation, which is the opposite of beginning in the middle.
a.clue: Is the background given before the action or after it?

b.q: Which opening is an example of in medias res?
opts: "Smoke filled the hall as Mia grabbed her brother's hand."
"Mia lived in a quiet town with her brother and parents."
"It was a bright Monday in March, and school had begun."
"This story begins with Mia's grandmother as a child."
b.why: The first opening starts in the middle of a crisis and leaves the reader to wonder how it began. The second is an orientation that sets out who and where before anything happens, so it does not begin in the middle.
b.clue: Look for the line where the action is already under way.
